chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Said from some of our companions from al-Mu'alla Abu 'Uthman from Abu Basir said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: 'And Dawud and Sulayman, when they judged concerning the field, when the sheep of the people grazed in it.'

He said: 'Grazing (nafash) occurs only at night. Indeed, it is upon the owner of the field to protect the field during the day, and it is not upon the owner of the livestock to protect them during the day; rather, their grazing and sustenance is during the day. So whatever they destroy [during the day], there is no liability upon them nor upon their owner. And it is upon the owner of the livestock to protect the livestock at night from the fields of the people. So whatever they destroy at night, they have guaranteed [liability], and that is the grazing.'

And indeed Dawud (peace be upon him) ruled for the one whose crop was damaged that the necks [bodies] of the sheep [should be given], and Sulayman ruled for the milk and the wool, and that was the milk and the wool for that year.'

key_terms.اَلنَّفْشُ: Grazing or browsing, specifically referring to the act of animals eating crops.
key_terms.اَلْمَاشِيَةُ: Livestock (specifically sheep and goats in this context).
key_terms.رِقَابُ: Necks, referring to the bodies of the animals given as compensation.

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling on livestock damaging crops during the day versus at night?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the jurisprudential basis for liability in crop damage by referencing the divine judgment of Prophets Dawud and Sulayman. It establishes a critical legal distinction where daytime grazing is considered natural usage with no liability, whereas nighttime damage implies negligence, making the owner fully liable for the loss. This ruling underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on contextualizing Quranic narratives to derive specific civil law principles regarding property rights and care obligations.
